---
title: "Set 14 — decision trees"
subtitle: "After lecture 16 · 23 November · about 40 minutes"
---

Data: [`churn.csv`](../materials/churn.csv) — 7 000 telecom customers, 28.5%
churn. Hold out 30% of the rows before you start and do not look at them again
until question 5. This exact split is used again in Sets 15 and 17:

```{.r}
churn <- read.csv("churn.csv", stringsAsFactors = TRUE)
churn$id <- NULL                                   # an identifier, not a predictor
set.seed(1)
idx   <- sample(nrow(churn), 0.7 * nrow(churn))
train <- churn[idx, ]                              # 4 900 rows
test  <- churn[-idx, ]                             # 2 100 rows, locked until question 5
```

Before you start: `set.seed(14)` right before the `rpart()` call — the Blackboard
test checks your numbers against this seed.

## 1 · Grow one, and read it aloud

Fit `rpart(churn ~ ., data = train, method = "class")` and plot it.

Write out the path to the leaf with the highest churn rate as an English
sentence a retention manager would understand. Report how many training
customers sit in that leaf.

## 2 · The first split is not an accident [In class]{.badge-class}

[We discuss this one in lecture 17, on 27 Nov — bring your answer.]{.muted}

Look at the root split.

Why did the algorithm choose that variable and that threshold, out of nineteen
columns and thousands of candidate cut points? Explain the criterion in terms of
impurity, not in terms of "it is the most important variable".

## 3 · Prune, with the table in front of you

`printcp` gives cross-validated error against complexity. Choose a tree with the
1-SE rule and one at the minimum `xerror`.

How many leaves does each have? Which would you deploy, and what exactly are you
trading?

## 4 · Instability, demonstrated [In class]{.badge-class}

[We discuss this one in lecture 17, on 27 Nov — bring your answer.]{.muted}

Refit the tree on a bootstrap sample of the training rows. Do it three times.

Does the root split change? Does the second level? Write two sentences on what
this implies for a sentence like *"the model says tenure is the key driver"*.

## 5 · The number you report

Now score the held-out 30% with your chosen tree: accuracy, and the confusion
matrix. For the Blackboard check, use the minimum-`xerror` tree.

Accuracy alone is flattering here. Say why, given the churn rate, and propose
the metric you would put in the report instead — with a reason tied to what the
company does with a prediction.

## Check yourself on Blackboard

Open the test **Set 14** on Blackboard and enter your numbers. Feedback appears
as soon as you submit. Nothing is graded, and you can take it as many times as
you like.

---

*This set checks: that a split has a criterion, that a tree is unstable by
construction, and that accuracy on an unbalanced target is a bad headline.*
